items.stem: Which is the best description of a scatter diagram whose points rise from left to right close to a line?
options: strong positive correlation
no correlation
strong negative correlation
weak negative correlation
items.answer: strong positive correlation
items.markingKey: A. Rising and close together.

items.stem: Sana writes: "A strong correlation proves that x causes y." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Correlation shows association, not cause.
items.markingKey: Correlation shows association, not cause. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Data show a strong positive correlation between ice-cream sales and sunburn cases. Ingrid concludes that ice-cream sales cause sunburn cases. Explain why this conclusion may be wrong.
items.answer: Both are likely to be affected by hot sunny weather (a lurking variable); correlation does not show causation.
items.markingKey: Correlation ≠ causation (R1); plausible third variable (R1).

items.stem: A study in Vienna recorded hours of revision (x) and test score (%) (y): (3, 37), (4, 48), (6, 45), (9, 60), (11, 69), (12, 73), (13, 89), (14, 76). Describe the correlation shown on a scatter diagram and interpret it in context.
items.answer: strong positive correlation
items.markingKey: strong positive correlation (A1 A1: direction and strength); interpretation – as hours of revision increases, test score (%) tends to increase (R1).

items.stem: Data for hours of revision (x) and test score (%) (y): (2, 29), (4, 0), (5, 49), (8, 61), (9, 72), (11, 75), (14, 88), (15, 95). (a) Identify the outlier. (b) Calculate r with and without it, to 3 d.p. (c) Comment on its effect.
items.answer: (a) (4, 0) (b) with: 0.897; without: 0.991 (c) the outlier weakens the correlation
items.markingKey: Outlier (A1); both r values from GDC (A1 A1); comment (R1).

items.stem: A student project in Seoul collected outside temperature (°C) (x) and heating bill (y) for 10 cases: (1, 151), (2, 146), (4, 152), (5, 131), (7, 129), (13, 94), (15, 83), (22, 72), (23, 52), (25, 51). (a) Identify the independent and dependent variables. (b) Describe the correlation. (c) Interpret it in context. (d) Explain one reason why you cannot conclude that x causes y.
items.answer: (a) independent: outside temperature (°C); dependent: heating bill (b) strong negative correlation (r ≈ −0.98) (c) as outside temperature (°C) increases, heating bill tends to decrease (d) e.g. a lurking variable or a small sample of 10 – the data show association, not proof of cause
items.markingKey: (a) independent: outside temperature (°C); dependent: heating bill (b) strong negative correlation (r ≈ −0.98) (c) as outside temperature (°C) increases, heating bill tends to decrease (d) e.g. a lurking variable or a small sample of 10 – the data show association, not proof of cause. Variables (A1); correlation described with direction and strength (A1 A1); interpretation (C1); critical reflection (D: R1).

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "Data with two variables measured for each item, which can be plotted as points (x, y)"?
options: independent variable
bivariate data
interpolation
line of best fit
items.answer: bivariate data
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of bivariate data.

items.stem: Briefly explain why correlation does not imply causation.
items.answer: Two variables can move together because of a third (lurking) variable or by coincidence; a link in data does not show that one causes the other.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Two variables can move together because of a third (lurking) variable or by coincidence; a link in data does not show that one causes the other. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims: "A strong correlation proves that x causes y." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Correlation shows association, not cause.
items.markingKey: Correlation shows association, not cause. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A study in Bogotá recorded screen time (hours) (x) and sleep (hours) (y): (1, 10), (2, 10), (3, 9), (4, 9), (5, 6), (6, 7), (7, 6), (8, 6). Describe the correlation shown on a scatter diagram and interpret it in context.
items.answer: strong negative correlation
items.markingKey: strong negative correlation (A1 A1: direction and strength); interpretation – as screen time (hours) increases, sleep (hours) tends to decrease (R1).

items.stem: Data for outside temperature (°C) (x) and heating bill (y): (0, 167), (1, 159), (6, 128), (16, 85), (17, 0), (18, 78), (23, 59), (25, 33). (a) Identify the outlier. (b) Calculate r with and without it, to 3 d.p. (c) Comment on its effect.
items.answer: (a) (17, 0) (b) with: −0.877; without: −0.994 (c) the outlier weakens the correlation
items.markingKey: Outlier (A1); both r values from GDC (A1 A1); comment (R1).

items.stem: A student project in Seoul collected outside temperature (°C) (x) and heating bill (y) for 10 cases: (0, 198), (4, 87), (6, 109), (7, 123), (11, 109), (13, 121), (16, 42), (18, 96), (19, 52), (20, 68). (a) Identify the independent and dependent variables. (b) Describe the correlation. (c) Interpret it in context. (d) Explain one reason why you cannot conclude that x causes y.
items.answer: (a) independent: outside temperature (°C); dependent: heating bill (b) strong negative correlation (r ≈ −0.75) (c) as outside temperature (°C) increases, heating bill tends to decrease (d) e.g. a lurking variable or a small sample of 10 – the data show association, not proof of cause
items.markingKey: (a) independent: outside temperature (°C); dependent: heating bill (b) strong negative correlation (r ≈ −0.75) (c) as outside temperature (°C) increases, heating bill tends to decrease (d) e.g. a lurking variable or a small sample of 10 – the data show association, not proof of cause. Variables (A1); correlation described with direction and strength (A1 A1); interpretation (C1); critical reflection (D: R1).

items.stem: In y = −3x + 50 (x = hours, y = battery %), the gradient means:
items.answer: the battery falls by 3% per hour
items.markingKey: the battery falls by 3% per hour. Gradient = rate of change.

items.stem: The line y = −2.2x + 72 models the price of a used phone (y, in dollars) against its age in months (x, data from 6 to 30 months). Explain what the y-intercept means and whether it is reliable.
items.answer: It predicts a price of 72 at age 0 (new); x = 0 is outside the data, so it is extrapolation and may not match the real new price.
items.markingKey: Meaning (A1); reliability (R1).

items.stem: Freya writes: "A line of best fit must go through the first and last points." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: It follows the overall trend, passing through the mean point, not particular points.
items.markingKey: It follows the overall trend, passing through the mean point, not particular points. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: For data on outside temperature (°C) (x) and heating bill (y) with x from 3 to 22, the regression line is y = −4.30x + 154. (a) Interpret the gradient. (b) Predict y for x = 16 and x = 45. (c) Comment on the reliability of each prediction.
items.answer: (a) y decreases by about 4.30 for each unit increase in x (b) 85.2; −39.5 (c) x = 16 is interpolation (reliable); x = 45 is extrapolation (unreliable)
items.markingKey: Gradient in context (R1); both predictions (A1 A1); interpolation vs extrapolation (R1).

items.stem: Data for hours of revision (x) and test score (%) (y): (1, 34), (2, 35), (5, 51), (6, 55), (11, 75), (12, 76), (14, 96). (a) Find the mean point. (b) Use technology to find the regression line y = ax + b (a, b to 3 s.f.). (c) Estimate y when x = 13.
items.markingKey: Mean point (A1); regression line (A1 A1); estimate by substitution (A1).

items.stem: Data for hours of revision (x) and test score (%) (y): (5, 54), (6, 58), (7, 57), (8, 72), (10, 70), (12, 88), (15, 94). (a) Find the mean point. (b) Use technology to find the regression line y = ax + b (a, b to 3 s.f.). (c) Estimate y when x = 8.
items.markingKey: Mean point (A1); regression line (A1 A1); estimate by substitution (A1).

items.stem: Researchers in Dubai recorded hours of revision (x) and test score (%) (y): (2, 42), (4, 48), (5, 45), (7, 64), (8, 72), (9, 64), (11, 85), (12, 86), (14, 94). (a) Find the mean point. (b) Find the equation of the regression line. (c) Show that the line passes through the mean point. (d) Predict y for x = 7 and x = 26, and comment on the reliability of each.
items.answer: (a) (8.00, 66.7) (b) y = 4.71x + 29.0 (c) check: 4.71 × 8.00 + 29.0 ≈ 66.7 = ȳ (d) x = 7: 62.0 (interpolation); x = 26: 151 (extrapolation – unreliable)
items.markingKey: (a) (8.00, 66.7) (b) y = 4.71x + 29.0 (c) check: 4.71 × 8.00 + 29.0 ≈ 66.7 = ȳ (d) x = 7: 62.0 (interpolation); x = 26: 151 (extrapolation – unreliable). Mean point and line (A1 A1 A1); verification (R1); predictions with reliability discussed (D: A1 R1).

items.stem: Researchers in Vienna recorded hours of revision (x) and test score (%) (y): (2, 30), (3, 38), (4, 52), (5, 50), (6, 53), (9, 68), (10, 68), (11, 83), (13, 86). (a) Find the mean point. (b) Find the equation of the regression line. (c) Show that the line passes through the mean point. (d) Predict y for x = 12 and x = 24, and comment on the reliability of each.
items.answer: (a) (7.00, 58.7) (b) y = 4.81x + 25.0 (c) check: 4.81 × 7.00 + 25.0 ≈ 58.7 = ȳ (d) x = 12: 82.7 (interpolation); x = 24: 140 (extrapolation – unreliable)
items.markingKey: (a) (7.00, 58.7) (b) y = 4.81x + 25.0 (c) check: 4.81 × 7.00 + 25.0 ≈ 58.7 = ȳ (d) x = 12: 82.7 (interpolation); x = 24: 140 (extrapolation – unreliable). Mean point and line (A1 A1 A1); verification (R1); predictions with reliability discussed (D: A1 R1).

items.stem: The line of best fit is y = 6x + 50. Predict y when x = 12.
Explain why interpolation is usually more reliable than extrapolation.
items.answer: Within the data we have evidence the trend holds; beyond the data the relationship might change.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Within the data we have evidence the trend holds; beyond the data the relationship might change. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Felix uses the regression line of y on x to predict x from a given y. Explain why this may give a poor estimate.
items.answer: The y-on-x line minimises vertical errors to predict y; predicting x needs the x-on-y line, which is different unless the correlation is perfect.
items.markingKey: Purpose of the line (R1); difference (R1).

items.stem: For data on hours of revision (x) and test score (%) (y) with x from 1 to 12, the regression line is y = 5.54x + 20.0. (a) Interpret the gradient. (b) Predict y for x = 10 and x = 25. (c) Comment on the reliability of each prediction.
items.answer: (a) y increases by about 5.54 for each unit increase in x (b) 75.4; 159 (c) x = 10 is interpolation (reliable); x = 25 is extrapolation (unreliable)
items.markingKey: Gradient in context (R1); both predictions (A1 A1); interpolation vs extrapolation (R1).

items.stem: For data on outside temperature (°C) (x) and heating bill (y) with x from 6 to 19, the regression line is y = −5.23x + 167. (a) Interpret the gradient. (b) Predict y for x = 15 and x = 25. (c) Comment on the reliability of each prediction.
items.answer: (a) y decreases by about 5.23 for each unit increase in x (b) 88.6; 36.3 (c) x = 15 is interpolation (reliable); x = 25 is extrapolation (unreliable)
items.markingKey: Gradient in context (R1); both predictions (A1 A1); interpolation vs extrapolation (R1).

items.stem: A student claims: "A line of best fit must go through the first and last points." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: It follows the overall trend, passing through the mean point, not particular points.
items.markingKey: It follows the overall trend, passing through the mean point, not particular points. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Researchers in Lima recorded hours of revision (x) and test score (%) (y): (2, 39), (3, 36), (4, 41), (6, 51), (9, 68), (10, 68), (13, 76), (14, 96), (15, 89). (a) Find the mean point. (b) Find the equation of the regression line. (c) Show that the line passes through the mean point. (d) Predict y for x = 10 and x = 28, and comment on the reliability of each.
items.answer: (a) (8.44, 62.7) (b) y = 4.39x + 25.6 (c) check: 4.39 × 8.44 + 25.6 ≈ 62.7 = ȳ (d) x = 10: 69.5 (interpolation); x = 28: 148 (extrapolation – unreliable)
items.markingKey: (a) (8.44, 62.7) (b) y = 4.39x + 25.6 (c) check: 4.39 × 8.44 + 25.6 ≈ 62.7 = ȳ (d) x = 10: 69.5 (interpolation); x = 28: 148 (extrapolation – unreliable). Mean point and line (A1 A1 A1); verification (R1); predictions with reliability discussed (D: A1 R1).

items.stem: Which value of r indicates the strongest linear correlation?
items.markingKey: B. |0.91| is largest.

items.stem: "r = 0.8 means 80% of the points are on the line." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: r measures closeness to a line overall; r² ≈ 0.64 is the proportion of variation explained.
items.markingKey: r measures closeness to a line overall; r² ≈ 0.64 is the proportion of variation explained. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why r is the same if x and y are swapped.
items.answer: The formula is symmetric in x and y: it measures how they vary together.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The formula is symmetric in x and y: it measures how they vary together. (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Use technology to find Pearson’s r for these data on screen time (hours) (x) and sleep (hours) (y): (1, 11), (2, 10), (3, 7), (4, 11), (7, 5), (8, 6). Give r to 3 d.p. and describe the correlation.
items.answer: r = −0.792; strong negative correlation
items.markingKey: r = −0.792 (A1 A1); description in terms of strength and direction (A1).

items.stem: For data on age of car (years) and value (thousands), r = −0.43. (a) Describe the correlation. (b) Find r² and interpret it.
items.answer: (a) weak negative correlation (b) r² = 0.185: about 18% of the variation in value (thousands) is explained by the linear relationship
items.markingKey: Description (A1); r² (A1); interpretation (R1).

items.stem: A school in Hanoi collected two data sets. Set 1, hours of revision vs test score (%): (3, 32), (4, 50), (5, 46), (7, 57), (8, 73), (10, 72), (11, 68), (15, 98). Set 2, shoe size vs mathematics score: (35, 82), (36, 68), (37, 51), (38, 77), (39, 84), (41, 73), (42, 73), (45, 58). (a) Find r for set 1. (b) Find r for set 2. (c) Describe each correlation. (d) For which set is a line of best fit useful for prediction? Justify.
items.answer: (a) r = 0.949 (b) r = −0.256 (c) set 1: strong positive correlation; set 2: weak negative correlation (d) a regression line is only useful for set 1, because |r| = 0.949 shows a strong linear correlation, while |r| = 0.256 for set 2 is too weak for reliable predictions
items.markingKey: (a) r = 0.949 (b) r = −0.256 (c) set 1: strong positive correlation; set 2: weak negative correlation (d) a regression line is only useful for set 1, because |r| = 0.949 shows a strong linear correlation, while |r| = 0.256 for set 2 is too weak for reliable predictions. Both r values (A1 A1); descriptions (A1 A1); justified conclusion (D: R1).

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "Pearson's correlation coefficient".
items.answer: R, a number from −1 to 1 measuring the strength and direction of a linear relationship
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: r, a number from −1 to 1 measuring the strength and direction of a linear relationship. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: For the points (-3, 9), (-2, 4), (-1, 1), (0, 0), (1, 1), (2, 4), (3, 9), r = 0. Alessia says the variables are unrelated. Explain why this is wrong.
items.answer: The points lie exactly on y = x², a perfect non-linear relationship; r only measures linear association.
items.markingKey: Non-linear pattern (R1); limitation of r (R1).

items.stem: "r = −0.9 is weaker than r = 0.5 because it is smaller." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Strength depends on |r|: 0.9 > 0.5, so −0.9 is stronger.
items.markingKey: Strength depends on |r|: 0.9 > 0.5, so −0.9 is stronger. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Use technology to find Pearson’s r for these data on hours of revision (x) and test score (%) (y): (1, 32), (2, 43), (3, 7), (5, 32), (6, 24), (8, 48), (11, 61), (13, 115). Give r to 3 d.p. and describe the correlation.
items.answer: r = 0.795; strong positive correlation
items.markingKey: r = 0.795 (A1 A1); description in terms of strength and direction (A1).

items.stem: For data on engine size (litres) and fuel used (L per 100 km), r = 0.31. (a) Describe the correlation. (b) Find r² and interpret it.
items.answer: (a) weak positive correlation (b) r² = 0.096: about 9.6% of the variation in fuel used (L per 100 km) is explained by the linear relationship
items.markingKey: Description (A1); r² (A1); interpretation (R1).

items.stem: A school in Singapore collected two data sets. Set 1, hours of revision vs test score (%): (1, 26), (3, 43), (5, 46), (6, 51), (7, 65), (10, 69), (11, 81), (12, 76). Set 2, shoe size vs mathematics score: (36, 77), (39, 92), (40, 88), (41, 44), (42, 76), (43, 67), (44, 73), (45, 86). (a) Find r for set 1. (b) Find r for set 2. (c) Describe each correlation. (d) For which set is a line of best fit useful for prediction? Justify.
items.answer: (a) r = 0.97 (b) r = −0.112 (c) set 1: strong positive correlation; set 2: very weak or no correlation (d) a regression line is only useful for set 1, because |r| = 0.97 shows a strong linear correlation, while |r| = 0.112 for set 2 is too weak for reliable predictions
items.markingKey: (a) r = 0.97 (b) r = −0.112 (c) set 1: strong positive correlation; set 2: very weak or no correlation (d) a regression line is only useful for set 1, because |r| = 0.97 shows a strong linear correlation, while |r| = 0.112 for set 2 is too weak for reliable predictions. Both r values (A1 A1); descriptions (A1 A1); justified conclusion (D: R1).

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "bias"?
options: R, a number from −1 to 1 measuring the strength and direction of a linear relationship
The case r = 1 or r = −1: all points lie exactly on a straight line
A systematic tendency for a sample or question to give results that differ from the truth about the population
A straight line that best represents the trend of the points on a scatter diagram
items.answer: A systematic tendency for a sample or question to give results that differ from the truth about the population
items.markingKey: C. "bias" is a systematic tendency for a sample or question to give results that differ from the truth about the population.

items.stem: A student claims: "Systematic sampling is always random." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: It is only random if the starting point is random and the list has no pattern.
items.markingKey: It is only random if the starting point is random and the list has no pattern. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: To estimate how often residents of Geneva exercise, a researcher surveys people leaving a gym. Identify the source of bias and suggest an improvement.
items.answer: Selection bias: gym users exercise more than average. Improvement: Survey at random from the electoral or postal register.
items.markingKey: Bias identified and explained (R1 A1); sensible improvement (A1).

items.stem: A survey in Accra uses a stratified sample of 60 from a population with 175 in Science, 120 in Arts, 59 in Business, 60 in Engineering. How many should be chosen from each group?
items.answer: Science: 25, Arts: 17, Business: 9, Engineering: 9
items.markingKey: Each group: size/414 × 60 (M1); 25.4, 17.4, 8.55, 8.70 (A1); rounded and total checked (A1).

items.stem: A school in Lisbon with 1500 students (444 lower school, 1056 upper school) wants to survey sleep. (a) Describe how to select a simple random sample of 60. (b) Find the numbers for a stratified sample of 60. (c) Write one unbiased question. (d) Identify one possible source of bias and how to reduce it.
items.answer: (a) number the students 1–1500 and choose 60 different random numbers (b) 17.8 → 18 lower-school and 42 upper-school students (c) e.g. a question on sleep with clear, non-overlapping options (d) e.g. non-response or untruthful answers; follow up and keep it anonymous
items.markingKey: (a) number the students 1–1500 and choose 60 different random numbers (b) 17.8 → 18 lower-school and 42 upper-school students (c) e.g. a question on sleep with clear, non-overlapping options (d) e.g. non-response or untruthful answers; follow up and keep it anonymous. Random method described (A1); stratified numbers (M1 A1); unbiased question (C1); bias discussed (D: R1).

items.stem: Explain why an online survey about internet use may be biased.
items.answer: Only people who use the internet can respond, so heavy users are over-represented.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Only people who use the internet can respond, so heavy users are over-represented. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain why a stratified sample by grade is suitable for a survey on homework time in a school.
items.answer: Homework time probably differs by grade; stratifying ensures each grade is represented in proportion.
items.markingKey: Strata linked to variable (R1); proportional representation (R1).

items.stem: A council in Melbourne asks: "Don’t you agree the new park is a waste of money?" Identify the source of bias and suggest an improvement.
items.answer: Leading question: it pushes respondents to agree. Improvement: Ask a neutral question, e.g. "How do you rate the new park from 1 to 5?"
items.markingKey: Bias identified and explained (R1 A1); sensible improvement (A1).

items.stem: A school in Mexico City with 1500 students (727 lower school, 773 upper school) wants to survey part-time work. (a) Describe how to select a simple random sample of 40. (b) Find the numbers for a stratified sample of 40. (c) Write one unbiased question. (d) Identify one possible source of bias and how to reduce it.
items.answer: (a) number the students 1–1500 and choose 40 different random numbers (b) 19.4 → 19 lower-school and 21 upper-school students (c) e.g. a question on part-time work with clear, non-overlapping options (d) e.g. non-response or untruthful answers; follow up and keep it anonymous
items.markingKey: (a) number the students 1–1500 and choose 40 different random numbers (b) 19.4 → 19 lower-school and 21 upper-school students (c) e.g. a question on part-time work with clear, non-overlapping options (d) e.g. non-response or untruthful answers; follow up and keep it anonymous. Random method described (A1); stratified numbers (M1 A1); unbiased question (C1); bias discussed (D: R1).

items.stem: Multiplying every value by 3 multiplies the standard deviation by:
items.markingKey: C. Distances from the mean triple.

items.stem: Felix writes: "Adding a constant to every value increases the standard deviation." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Every value moves equally, so the spread is unchanged.
items.markingKey: Every value moves equally, so the spread is unchanged. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Sets A = 25, 26, 26, 27 and B = 18, 24, 28, 34 both have mean 26. Explain, using standard deviation, how they differ.
items.answer: σ_A ≈ 0.707 and σ_B ≈ 5.83: B is much more spread out; the mean alone does not describe spread.
items.markingKey: Both σ (A1); comparison (R1).

items.stem: The table shows the number of siblings: value 0, 1, 2, 3, 4; frequency 6, 2, 12, 10, 5. Find the mean and standard deviation to 3 s.f.
items.markingKey: Σf = 35, Σfx = 76 (M1); mean (A1); σ from GDC with frequencies (A1 A1).

items.stem: The heights of seedlings (cm) recorded in Mexico City were: 19, 39, 24, 32, 6, 14, 22. Use technology to find the mean and the (population) standard deviation, to 3 s.f.

Investigate how transformations affect the mean and standard deviation of 30, 22, 20, 22, 27, 26. (a) Find the mean and σ. (b) Add 5 to every value and find them again. (c) Multiply every original value by 3 and find them again. (d) State general rules.
items.answer: (a) mean 24.5, σ 3.45 (b) adding 5: mean 29.5, σ 3.45 (c) × 3: mean 73.5, σ 10.4 (d) adding shifts the mean only; multiplying scales both
items.markingKey: (a) mean 24.5, σ 3.45 (b) adding 5: mean 29.5, σ 3.45 (c) × 3: mean 73.5, σ 10.4 (d) adding shifts the mean only; multiplying scales both. Statistics computed (A1 A1 A1); comparison / pattern (B/D: R1); communication (C1).

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "variance".
items.answer: The square of the standard deviation, σ²
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the square of the standard deviation, σ². Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Briefly explain why a smaller standard deviation means more consistent data.
items.answer: The values lie closer to the mean on average.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The values lie closer to the mean on average. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: The daily rainfall (mm) recorded in Oslo were: 22, 18, 32, 16, 10, 40, 28. Use technology to find the mean and the (population) standard deviation, to 3 s.f.
"Adding a constant to every value increases the standard deviation." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Every value moves equally, so the spread is unchanged.
items.markingKey: Every value moves equally, so the spread is unchanged. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Data set A (masses (g) of bags filled by machine A): 500, 502, 502, 503, 500, 502, 497, 503. Data set B (masses (g) of bags filled by machine B): 503, 494, 498, 500, 501, 502, 508, 492.
